claims.text: The conventionally cast eutectic high-entropy alloy has coarse dual-phase lamellar colonies.
Internal boundaries in the conventionally cast alloy are common microcrack-initiation sites.
Rapid solidification can produce a finer and more homogeneous lamellar microstructure than conventional casting.
Rapid solidification enhances interfacial bonding between the two phases.
Finer lamellar spacing lowers stress concentrations at internal boundaries.
Lower boundary stress concentrations delay microcrack initiation and propagation.
Lamellar refinement improves load transfer between the two phases.
Lamellar refinement produces a more uniform strain distribution during room-temperature tensile deformation.
Rapid solidification will increase yield strength relative to the conventionally cast baseline.
Rapid solidification will increase room-temperature tensile ductility relative to the conventionally cast baseline.
The simultaneous increases in yield strength and ductility overcome the usual strength-ductility trade-off.
The predicted improvement is conditional on retaining the dual-phase structure while avoiding amorphous or brittle secondary phases.
The predicted improvement is conditional on minimizing phase segregation.

contradictions.description: The boundary excludes processing conditions that introduce amorphous or brittle secondary phases, but the falsification rule treats the emergence of brittle phases as falsifying the bounded hypothesis. Such a result would instead show that the intervention failed to satisfy its stated boundary conditions unless phase formation is explicitly treated as an unavoidable consequence of the tested rapid-solidification window.
